extracted.intended_audience: literary critics, reviewers, and poets (readers assessing and writing poetry)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for conducting fair, philosophical, and effective critical reviews of poetry (illustrated via discussion of Wordsworth), and standards for poetic style and composition to be judged or practised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fair and philosophical inquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic should conduct 'a fair and philosophical inquisition into the character of [a poet], as a poet, on the evidence of his published works; and a positive, not a comparative, appreciation of their characteristic excellencies, deficiencies, and defects.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Announce and establish the general principles you hold for poetry, specify how those principles apply to different classes of poetry, particularize striking passages to which you deem them applicable, note recurrence of merits or defects, and distinguish what is characteristic from what is accidental. If premises are rational and deductions legitimate, readers (and authors) can adopt the judgment; if wrong, present errors in a definite place and tangible form to guide detection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Announce canons and apply them to particulars
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic 'announces and endeavours to establish the principles, which he holds for the foundation of poetry in general, with the specification of these in their application to the different classes of poetry.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prepare canons of criticism for praise and condemnation, then particularize passages and indicate frequency and context. Explicit principles enable rational deductions and transparent critique rather than vague denunciation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground verdicts in argument and evidence, not assertion
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'the substitution of assertion for argument' and 'arbitrary and sometimes petulant verdicts, not seldom unsupported even by a single quotation from the work condemned.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support judgments with quotations and general grounds that show why the fault is attributable to the passage; extracts should illustrate general rules. Do not write critique before reading and then pick passages merely to illustrate preconceived opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select passages that genuinely illustrate the point
rubrics_metrics.description: When extracting lines to support a judgment, ensure the extracts 'explain the critic’s meaning, if it did not prove the justice of his sentence.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cherry-picking isolated lines that contradict the author's intention or that the critic acknowledges to be beautiful; connect extracts to an established principle or rule rather than using them as rhetorical provocation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep criticism impersonal — censure the work, not the author
rubrics_metrics.description: Every just censure of a publication 'is the critic’s right' but 'as soon as the critic betrays, that he knows more of his author, than the author’s publications could have told him... his censure instantly becomes personal injury... He ceases to be a critic, and takes on him the most contemptible character... a gossip, backbiter, and pasquillant.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Address the work in front of you. Do not avail yourself of private knowledge or allude to personal traits; avoid personal malignity, wantonness, or re-committing forgotten juvenile performances to public notice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unlicensed personality or private malignity
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic must not use private grudges or malignity to force back forgotten works into public notice or to attack the author's person rather than the work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exclude personal allusions; when censure rests on knowledge beyond the publications, it becomes illegitimate. If criticism must be keen or asperous, direct it at the impersonated work, not the man.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know the effect you intend and weigh your tone
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic 'must know, what effect it is his object to produce; and with a view to this effect must he weigh his words.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose phrasing (soft/hard, friendly/bitter) to suit intended rhetorical effect; be deliberate about asperity only insofar as it serves a justified critical purpose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain impartiality — set aside party and predilection
rubrics_metrics.description: Set aside 'the too manifest and too frequent interference of national party, and even personal predilection or aversion' when conducting reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ground judgments on reason and universal morals rather than on national, political, or personal bias; reserve legal remedies only for criminal intrusions into private life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review what merits argumentative criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Periodical criticism should 'review those books only, which are susceptible and deserving of argumentative criticism' and replace trivial works with original essays on important subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid devoting critical labour to trifling publications merely to fill space or pander to malicious passions; prioritise works that invite reasoned debate and exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not resurrect or re-try juvenile performances unfairly
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics should avoid 're-commitment (for new trial) of juvenile performances, that were published, perhaps forgotten, many years before the commencement of the review.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bringing long-forgotten youthful works back into current condemnation is often motivated by spite or desire for notoriety; avoid this practice unless there is clear literary justification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid substituting personality for public argument
rubrics_metrics.description: When the critic 'from more intimate knowledge, elsewhere obtained, avails himself of the slightest trait against the author; his censure instantly becomes personal insult.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep the museum (public literary domain) free of private quarrels; personal attacks degrade criticism into gossip and profane the 'altar of the Muses.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain tonal and stylistic consistency in a poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid 'the inconstancy of the style' — sudden and unprepared transitions from lines of 'peculiar felicity' to a style 'not only unimpassioned but undistinguished.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not alternate jarringly between language peculiar to poetry and neutral/common language without preparation; frequent abrupt shifts produce a feeling of disharmony, anticlimax, or hyperclimax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prepare the reader for stylistic shifts; structure elements for effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The critic recommends managing contrasts as Metastasio did by placing the aria at the end of the scene and raising the style of the recitative immediately preceding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When combining different registers (song/recitative, poetic/neutral), arrange and elevate surrounding material so transitions feel natural and expected rather than startling.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid matter-of-factness and excessive minuteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not indulge in 'a matter-of-factness' manifested as 'laborious minuteness and fidelity in the representation of objects' or insertion of accidental circumstances necessary only in real-life explanation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poetry should be 'the most intense, weighty and philosophical product of human art' — avoid over-detailed local imagery that makes the reader reconstruct a map piece by piece; be economical and selective in descriptive detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paint to the imagination; create co-presence of the whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should 'paint to the imagination, not to the fancy' — create an image with 'co-presence of the whole picture flashed at once upon the eye' rather than a dissected series of parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for creation rather than mere painting of particulars: give the reader an instant, unified apprehension (as in Milton's passages), not a sequence of separately examined details that require mental reassembly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid superfluous accidental circumstances
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include details ('circumstances') that might be necessary to establish probability in real life but are superfluous in poetry where the reader is willing to believe for the sake of the poem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Trim incidental facts that burden a poetic narrative; include only what contributes to the poem's imaginative truth or necessity of the tale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be wary of unusual diction not used in ordinary speech
rubrics_metrics.description: Question whether 'those words in those places [are] commonly employed in real life to express the same thought or outward thing' — avoid diction that is not used in ordinary intercourse unless justified by poetic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of awkward poetic diction include turns like 'the thrush is busy in the wood?' or 'both earth and sky keep jubilee!' Use of archaic or forced phrases can alienate readers unless the poet consciously chooses a heightened diction and accepts the trade-offs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with peculiar grammatical constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Note peculiar frequent constructions (e.g., 'the asymartaeton... and... the construction of words by apposition — “to him, a youth”') and assess whether they serve or harm poetic expression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such constructions may be effective in moderation but can seem artificial if overused; evaluate whether their omission would rob the poem of marked beauties or whether they are gratuitous departures from natural syntax.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow for experiments but measure influence and proportion
rubrics_metrics.description: If a poet has set forth principles that are insufficiently supported and which may have influenced compositions, 'let the effects be pointed out, and the instances given... whether the number and importance of the poems and passages thus infected be great or trifling... and lastly, whether they are inwoven into the texture of his works, or are loose and separable.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticizing theoretical stances, distinguish between occasional experimental failures and pervasive defects; measure scope, frequency, and whether problematic elements are integral or detachable.
